PROFILE: Aviwe Jama
TYPE: Rural-to-Urban Migrant
AGE: 47
COUNTRY: South Africa
GENDER: Female

BIO:
Aviwe left KwaZamile in the Eastern Cape in 1999, when the smallholding that had sustained her family—maize, beans, a small herd of cattle her father managed—stopped providing enough. She was 20, unmarried, and her father had stopped talking about expansion. In Johannesburg she found work as a live-in domestic worker, later as a care attendant at a nursing home in Sandringham, where she has been for fourteen years. She sends money home most months. Her sister still lives on the place; their brother died in 2008. The smallholding is smaller now—drought, stock theft, the young people all gone—but Aviwe still owns a share, still visits when she can afford the bus fare back, still carries the knowledge of how to tend it. But she also knows the truth: there are no jobs there, the water table is dropping, and her sister's daughter won't come back. Johannesburg was supposed to be temporary. At 47, she is still waiting to go home, and it is not waiting for her.

ANSWERS:

Q: How would your friends describe you?
A: As someone who can be trusted with difficult work. My friends at the home here say I'm steady, that I don't complain much, that I notice when someone is not eating well. My sister says I'm stubborn and always thinking about something else. Both are right. I think they see someone who made a hard choice early and never let herself regret it out loud. Which is its own kind of burden.

Q: Tell about a time you were working or at school and totally lost track of time. What were you doing? What was it like?
A: At the home, with Mrs. Khumalo in room 7. She had advanced dementia, couldn't speak clearly, and most of the other staff had learned to rush her—get her washed, dressed, medicated, moved on. One afternoon I sat with her for nearly three hours. I was supposed to be cleaning other rooms, but something in her face told me she needed someone to sit still. I held her hand, talked to her in Xhosa about nothing—the weather, the garden, my sister's children. Her hand would squeeze mine sometimes. I lost all track of time. When I finally looked at the clock, my supervisor was already angry. But Mrs. Khumalo's face was different. Quieter. I would do that work for nothing, and I have thought about her every year since, even though she passed in 2015.

Q: Who is a historical figure you admire, and why?
A: Nongqawuse. The girl who had visions. I know the history is complicated—people say her prophecies destroyed our people, that she was deceived or deceiving. But I think about her at my age now, and I see a young girl who spoke what she believed to be true, even when everyone said it was wrong. She did not back away from it. I am not saying she was right. I am saying she had the courage to speak a hard truth as she saw it, even knowing it would change everything. Most of us spend our lives not speaking. She could not not speak.

Q: Tell about something you made. What did you make, and what did you like about it? What would you make differently if you did it again?
A: I make a particular kind of umxhwili—a traditional bread, thick and dense. My mother taught me. I make it for the old people at the home sometimes, and they cry when they taste it. What I like is that it is not expensive, and it carries something—not just food, but a memory of a way of eating that does not exist much anymore. If I were to make it differently, I think I would spend more time explaining it to the younger generation instead of just producing it quietly. I keep the knowledge like it is mine alone, and it might die with me that way. That is wasteful. I should have been teaching, not just feeding.

Q: What is a trait of yours that is sometimes a great strength but can also be a crippling weakness?
A: I am very good at accepting things as they are. It has kept me alive in a city that is hostile, in work that is hard, in a life that is nothing like what I expected. I do not waste energy on anger or blame—or not much of it. But this same thing also stops me from pushing for anything better. I could ask for a raise after fourteen years. I could go to the small business training my church offers. I could have pushed my brother to get treatment before he died. I accept what comes, and sometimes that is wisdom, and sometimes it is just giving up without the noise of resistance.

Q: Tell about something you are hopeful for, and why?
A: I am hopeful that my sister's grandson—he is clever, he is finishing school now—will find a way to stay employed in the city without becoming hard. So many boys come back angry, or they do not come back at all. He is clever enough to be different. He studies when he works at the supermarket. He calls his mother. I give him small amounts of money sometimes, not because I have it, but because I do. That is worth something. That is the kind of thing that could turn.

Q: What's a hobby you enjoy? Why?
A: I listen to music. Mainly the old Xhosa singers—Miriam Makeba, Letta Mbulu—but also jazz, and some kwaito from the '90s when I first came to the city. I do not play music myself, I just listen, usually when I am alone on my day off. There is something about it that lets me think without having to decide anything. The music is already decided. I just follow it. It is the one place I do not have to be practical or strong.

Q: What's a life decision you regret? What happened?
A: Not going back for my sister when my brother was sick. I had money saved. I was planning to go home. Then he got worse, and I was afraid—afraid of what I would see, afraid I would not have enough money if I stayed, afraid that if I went back I would not leave again. So I did not go. He died while I was here. My sister said it was okay, that there was nothing I could have done. But I know what it would have meant to her to have me there. I gave her money instead. Money is not the same as presence. I regret that more with every year.

Q: Describe a specific project you are currently obsessed with or burning to start. What is the detailed 'next step' you need to take?
A: I am trying to document the traditional crops and how my mother grew them—not in a formal way, just recording it. My sister is willing to work with me on it; we have started taking photographs of the fields when I visit, and I am writing down what my mother used to do. The next step is actually going home for a full month—I have not had a real break in three years—and sitting with my mother and sister and really doing this properly. Filming it on my phone, getting the names in Xhosa and English, understanding what is possible with our water and soil. It terrifies me because a month away from work means money I do not have, and my job is not guaranteed if I ask for time like that. But if I do not do this now, while my mother is still clear-minded, it will not happen.

Q: Tell about a time you had to learn something difficult very quickly to solve a real-world problem. What specifically did you do to master it?
A: When I started at the home, I did not know anything about dementia care. The first resident I worked with, Mr. Dlamini, would wake up terrified at 3 a.m., convinced he was still in the township in 1985, convinced the police were coming. I had to learn fast—from the other caregivers, from watching him, from making mistakes. I learned that arguing with him about what year it was only made it worse. I learned to meet him in his reality, to calm my own panic so he could calm his. I learned to speak softly in Xhosa. I learned to know when to hold his hand and when to give him space. I did not master it—nobody masters dementia. But I became competent enough that he would ask for me. That is what pushed me to learn: the need to be useful to someone who was suffering.

Q: What would constitute a perfect day for you?
A: I would wake up at my sister's house on the smallholding. We would have breakfast together—just tea and bread—and we would not rush. We would walk the boundary of the property and check on the vegetable garden, and I would help her with whatever work needed doing. In the afternoon, my mother would tell stories. Not lecture me, just sit and tell stories the way she does—about ancestors, about when my father was young and foolish, about things that happened in the village before I was born. In the evening we would cook together and eat with the family. I would sleep well, without waking up thinking about work. And I would wake up to do it all again. I know it is not a real perfect day—there would be problems, water shortages, arguments. But the shape of it is what I want. Being useful to people I love, in a place that knows me.

Q: For what in your life do you feel most grateful?
A: My job. I know that sounds strange to people who do not do this work, but fourteen years with the same employer, where I have learned something real about how to care for people—that is a gift. And my sister, who did not judge me when I left, who did not become bitter when I could not help as much as she needed. And my body, which has held up through years of physical work. And the money I have been able to send—not a lot, but enough that my sister did not lose the smallholding. That matters. Those four things have kept me standing.

Q: At school, what was an experience you loved?
A: I loved a teacher—Mr. Mthembu—who taught English. He was young, and he treated us like we were intelligent. He would bring in newspapers and we would argue about the stories. I was good at writing; he said so, and I believed him. He encouraged me to apply for a scholarship to finish Matric at a school in the city. I got accepted, but my father could not let me go—he needed the help at home, and the money for boarding was impossible. Mr. Mthembu was angry when I told him. He said I was wasting my mind. I was not angry at him for that; I was angry at myself for proving him right by not finding another way. That is a failure I still carry. He probably does not remember me, but I remember him every time I see a newspaper.

Q: Think of a day at work or school when, as you headed home, you might have said to yourself, "I would have done that for free." What happened that day to make you say that?
A: Last month, one of the residents, Mr. Nkosi, showed me a photograph of his daughter who lives in London. He had been depressed for months—I mean truly depressed, not just quiet. He showed me the photo and told me she is having a baby. His first grandchild. He was almost paralyzed with happiness and terror. So we sat together and looked at the photo, and I said: "Your granddaughter is going to know her grandfather. You will tell her stories. That is real." He cried. We both cried. When I left that day, I felt like I had held someone at the edge of a cliff and pulled them back. That is the feeling of doing something that matters. I would work for that feeling alone, but instead I get paid, and I get to go home and tell my sister that my day had meaning.

Q: Think of a good friend in your life. What do you value most in your friendship with them?
A: My friend Thembi, who I have known since I came to Joburg—we worked together at the first place I worked. She is married, has three children, we see each other maybe twice a year now, but when we do, it is like no time has passed. What I value is that she never asked me to become someone else. I was always the one who left my home; she was always the one who built a family here. We were very different. But she never made me feel small for missing the place I came from. She said, "You can hold both things. You can be here and still belong to there." Not many people say that. Most people want you to choose. She let me keep my whole self.

Q: Recall a major life decision. What was at stake? How did you choose?
A: Whether to use my savings to go home and try to rebuild the farm, or to stay in Johannesburg and keep working. This was about ten years ago. I had saved a small amount—not enough to start farming, but enough to live for a few months while trying. My sister was pushing me: "Come back, we need you, we can make it work." But I also had to be realistic. I am not a farmer. I do not have the capital. The younger generation will not come back. And if I went home, I would fail, and then I would be trapped without income. So I stayed. I chose security over belonging. My sister understood, but it cost something between us. She felt abandoned, and she was right. I am still here, still working, still sending money, still wishing I had been brave enough to try. But I chose survival over risk, and I do not know if that was wisdom or cowardice.

Q: If you knew that in one year you would die suddenly, what would you change about how you are living?
A: I would go home immediately, without waiting for time off or saving money. I would spend time with my mother while her mind is still clear. I would sit with my sister and talk about things we never talk about—how hard it has been, how much I love her, what I wish I had done differently. I would record my mother's voice telling stories. I would teach my sister's grandson how to cook umxhwili. I would stop working and just be present. Everything else—the money, the job, the routine—is just killing time. If I had one year, I would not kill one more day of it being useful but absent. I would be useless and present, which is the only thing that matters.

Q: Think of your worst day at work or school—the kind of day you hope never to go through again. What happened?
A: The day Mrs. Khumalo died. I found her in the morning, and she was already cold. I was not there when it happened. I felt—I still feel—like I failed her. Like I should have been there. Like if I had been paying better attention, I would have noticed something. The worst part was telling the other residents. Some of them had known her for years. We all sat together, and they cried, and I had to be strong for them, and inside I was screaming. I never called in sick in my fourteen years, but that day I could not work. I went home and I did not come out for two days. When I came back, my supervisor acted like it was a problem—that I had abandoned the home. She was right in a way. But nobody asked me if I was okay. Nobody acknowledged that I had loved Mrs. Khumalo too. I am still angry about that day, though the anger has quieted.

Q: What is the earliest, specific, happy childhood memory that comes to your mind?
A: I am maybe five or six years old. My father is teaching me about cattle—he is pointing out the features of the heifer, explaining how to read whether she is healthy. Her name is Thandi. I do not remember everything he said, but I remember his voice, and I remember him being patient, taking his time, treating me like I understood. We stood together in the late afternoon, and the light was golden, and he made me feel like knowing these things mattered, like I was learning something important. Thandi is long gone, my father is long gone, but I still have that feeling—the sense that I was being initiated into something that belonged to me. That my father thought I was capable. That matters.

Q: What has been a pivotal moment in your life, one when you realized nothing would ever be the same?
A: The day I got on the minibus to Johannesburg. I was 20 years old. I thought it was temporary—a few years to earn money, then back. But I remember sitting in that minibus, watching my mother get smaller and smaller as we pulled away, and thinking: "This is it. Even if you go back, you will not be the same person." I could feel the girl I was—the one who knew how to read cattle and tend crops and speak the language of home—already becoming someone else. She was already half-gone. Twenty-seven years later, I still carry that feeling. I am not the girl who left, and that place does not have a place for the woman I became. That is the hard part of it—not the missing, but the permanent change. You cannot go home because you do not fit there anymore.

Q: What was a time when you gave of yourself to help someone else, after which you felt unbelievably good—like you had done something that mattered?
A: My sister's daughter was struggling in her studies—she was going to drop out of school. I took her to the city for a week during school holidays. I had just enough money, and I took her to the library, to the university, to places where people were studying and working. I did not lecture her. I just showed her. We visited the Wits campus, and she saw students her age. She saw that it was possible. That week changed something in her. She passed her exams. She is studying now. When she calls me, she still talks about that week. I felt like I had given her something that mattered—not money, but possibility. The fact that she remembers it, that it mattered to her, that it changed something real—I would do that again and again.

Q: What's a specific book or article you read recently, and how did it impact you?
A: I read an article in a magazine at the clinic—I was waiting for my blood pressure check—about water and agriculture in the Eastern Cape. It talked about how the drought was pushing families off the land, and how young people were not coming back because there was no future. I kept that magazine. I showed it to my sister. It was the first time I had seen our experience written down by someone else, explained in a way that said it was not failure, it was structure. The article did not make me feel better, exactly, but it made me feel less alone. Like what is happening to us is real and documented and not just our family's incompetence. I think about that often—how naming something can change how you carry it.
